text: The report is built and connected. This lesson is about the last, easy-to-skip step: actually presenting it to the person who asked for it, in a way that holds up after you leave the room.

The VP asked for one thing, so two visuals answer it completely. A line chart, with the day on one axis and the ticket count on the other, one line per priority — the shape of the month, at a glance. And a matrix table, day by priority, with the exact numbers behind that chart, for whenever the VP wants to check a specific day.

That's it, on purpose. No KPI cards nobody asked for, no extra breakdown by channel or status. Adding those now would be the exact same scope creep Lesson one warned about — it's just showing up at the finish line instead of the start.

A good walkthrough for a report this size takes two minutes, not twenty. State the question in the VP's own words. Point at the line chart first — the shape of the month, and anything that jumps out. Show the matrix as backup, for the exact number behind any one day. And say plainly what refresh actually does: pulls whatever's currently loaded in Snowflake.

Here's the real test of done. Not whether the dashboard looks nice — whether the VP can open this themselves next week, find the number they need without calling you, and trust it because they roughly understand how it's built. That's a higher bar, and it's the actual payoff of every scoping decision made back in lesson one.

The report is built, presented, and trusted. Last lesson, we step back and recap exactly what this project built — and look ahead to what changes once Driftwood has more than one stakeholder asking questions.
